sanskrit_shloka:
घेरण्ड उवाच ।
अथाऽतः संप्रवक्ष्यामि प्रत्याहारमनुत्तमम् ।
यस्य विज्ञानमात्रेण कामादिरिपुनाशनम् ॥
text:
घेरण्ड उवाच ।
अथाऽतः संप्रवक्ष्यामि प्रत्याहारमनुत्तमम् ।
यस्य विज्ञानमात्रेण कामादिरिपुनाशनम् ॥
transliteration:
gheraṇḍa uvāca |
athā'taḥ saṃpravakṣyāmi pratyāhāramanuttamam |
yasya vijñānamātreṇa kāmādiripunāśanam ||
translation: Gheranda said: Now, therefore, I shall fully expound the unsurpassed Pratyahara (sensory withdrawal), by the mere knowledge and practice of which the internal enemies such as lust, anger, and other desires are completely destroyed.

translations.author: English Translation
translations.description: Gheranda said: Now, therefore, I shall fully expound the unsurpassed Pratyahara (sensory withdrawal), by the mere knowledge and practice of which the internal enemies such as lust, anger, and other desires are completely destroyed.

translations.author: Hindi Translation (भावार्थ)
translations.description: घेरण्ड ने कहा: अब इसके पश्चात्, मैं उस सर्वोत्तम (सर्वोत्कृष्ट) प्रत्याहार का सम्यक् वर्णन करूँगा, जिसके मात्र ज्ञान और अभ्यास से काम-क्रोध आदि शत्रुओं का नाश हो जाता है।

commentary_faqs.question: Practice: Pratyahara
commentary_faqs.answer: Sensory withdrawal as a tool to destroy internal afflictions and passions (Kama, Krodha, etc.)

commentary_faqs.question: Therapeutic & Somatic Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: Pratyahara helps in treating modern psychological and lifestyle issues such as sensory overload, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), chronic stress, anxiety, and addictive behaviors by training the mind to disconnect from external stressors.

sanskrit_shloka:
यतो यतो निश्चरति मनश्चञ्चलमस्थिरम् ।
ततस्ततो नियम्यैतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत् ॥
text:
यतो यतो निश्चरति मनश्चञ्चलमस्थिरम् ।
ततस्ततो नियम्यैतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत् ॥
transliteration:
yato yato niścarati manaścañcalamasthiram |
tatastato niyamyaitadātmanyeva vaśaṁ nayet ||
translation: From whatever cause or direction the restless and unsteady mind wanders away, one should restrain it from that and bring it back under the control of the Self alone.

translations.author: English Translation
translations.description: From whatever cause or direction the restless and unsteady mind wanders away, one should restrain it from that and bring it back under the control of the Self alone.

translations.description: यह चंचल और अस्थिर मन जिस-जिस विषय के कारण बाहर भटकता है, उस-उस से इसे रोककर (खींचकर) अपने वश में करते हुए आत्मा में ही स्थापित करना चाहिए।
translations.text: यह चंचल और अस्थिर मन जिस-जिस विषय के कारण बाहर भटकता है, उस-उस से इसे रोककर (खींचकर) अपने वश में करते हुए आत्मा में ही स्थापित करना चाहिए।

commentary_faqs.question: Practice: Pratyahara
commentary_faqs.answer: Restraint of the unsteady mind (Manonigraha) and its redirection from external sensory stimuli back into the inner Self.

commentary_faqs.question: Therapeutic & Somatic Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This technique of conscious sensory withdrawal and mental anchoring is highly effective in treating modern lifestyle disorders such as chronic anxiety, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), clinical stress, and psychosomatic ailments by downregulating the sympathetic nervous system.

sanskrit_shloka:
यत्र यत्र गता दृष्टिर्मनस्तत्र प्रगच्छति ।
ततः प्रत्याहरेदेतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत् ॥
text:
यत्र यत्र गता दृष्टिर्मनस्तत्र प्रगच्छति ।
ततः प्रत्याहरेदेतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत् ॥
transliteration:
yatra yatra gatā dṛṣṭirmanastatra pragacchati |
tataḥ pratyāharedetadātmanyeva vaśaṃ nayet ||
translation: Wherever the gaze goes, the mind wanders there too. One should withdraw the mind/gaze from all those objects, and bring it under absolute control in the Self alone.

translations.author: English Translation
translations.description: Wherever the gaze goes, the mind wanders there too. One should withdraw the mind/gaze from all those objects, and bring it under absolute control in the Self alone.

translations.description: जहाँ-जहाँ भी दृष्टि जाती है, मन भी वहीं-वहीं चला जाता है। अतः उस-उस स्थान से इसे (मन और दृष्टि को) वापस खींचना चाहिए और इसे अपने वश में करके आत्मा में ही लीन करना चाहिए।
translations.text: जहाँ-जहाँ भी दृष्टि जाती है, मन भी वहीं-वहीं चला जाता है। अतः उस-उस स्थान से इसे (मन और दृष्टि को) वापस खींचना चाहिए और इसे अपने वश में करके आत्मा में ही लीन करना चाहिए।

commentary_faqs.question: Practice: Pratyahara (Sensory Withdrawal)
commentary_faqs.answer: The intrinsic connection between the senses (specifically sight/Drishti) and the mind (Manas). Control of the mind is achieved by consciously redirecting outward attention back into the internal Self.

commentary_faqs.question: Therapeutic & Somatic Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This practice is highly effective in treating modern psychological issues such as attention deficits (ADHD), chronic stress, anxiety, and sensory overload caused by digital overstimulation. By training the mind to disconnect from external visual and mental distractions, the sympathetic nervous system is quieted, promoting deep mental restoration and cognitive focus.

sanskrit_shloka:
पुरस्कारं तिरस्कारं सुश्राव्यं दुःश्रुतं तथा ।
मनस्तस्मान्नियम्यैतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत् ॥
text:
पुरस्कारं तिरस्कारं सुश्राव्यं दुःश्रुतं तथा ।
मनस्तस्मान्नियम्यैतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत् ॥
transliteration:
puraskāraṁ tiraskāraṁ suśrāvyaṁ duḥśrutaṁ tathā |
manastas mān niyamya tādātmany eva vaśaṁ nayet ||
translation: Whether receiving praise (honor) or insult (dishonor), and whether hearing words that are pleasant or unpleasant, one should restrain the mind from those external triggers and bring it completely under control within the Self alone.

translations.author: English Translation
translations.description: Whether receiving praise (honor) or insult (dishonor), and whether hearing words that are pleasant or unpleasant, one should restrain the mind from those external triggers and bring it completely under control within the Self alone.

translations.description: मान-सम्मान (पुरस्कार) या अपमान (तिरस्कार) मिलने पर, तथा मधुर (सुश्राव्य) या कटु (दुःश्रुत) वचनों को सुनने पर भी, मन को उन बाह्य विषयों से हटाकर नियंत्रित करना चाहिए और उसे अपनी आत्मा के ही वश में लाना चाहिए।

commentary_faqs.question: Practice: Pratyahara
commentary_faqs.answer: Withdrawal of mind from sensory dualities (honor/dishonor, praise/blame, pleasant/unpleasant sounds)

commentary_faqs.question: Therapeutic & Somatic Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: Stress management, emotional dysregulation, anxiety, depressive states, and personality disorders by cultivating cognitive resilience and equanimity (Samatvam) against external emotional triggers.

sanskrit_shloka:
शीतं वाऽपि तथा चोष्णं यन्मनःस्पर्शयोगतः ।
तस्मात्प्रत्याहरेदेतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत् ॥
text:
शीतं वाऽपि तथा चोष्णं यन्मनःस्पर्शयोगतः ।
तस्मात्प्रत्याहरेदेतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत् ॥
transliteration:
śītaṃ vā'pi tathā coṣṇaṃ yanmanaḥsparśayogataḥ ।
tasmātpratyāharedetadātmanyeva vaśaṃ nayet ॥
translation: Whatever cold or heat is experienced through the contact of the mind with the senses, one should withdraw the mind from those objects and bring it under control, centering it in the Self alone.

translations.author: English Translation
translations.description: Whatever cold or heat is experienced through the contact of the mind with the senses, one should withdraw the mind from those objects and bring it under control, centering it in the Self alone.

commentary_faqs.question: Practice: Pratyahara
commentary_faqs.answer: Sensory withdrawal from dualities (such as heat and cold) to establish mental absorption in the Self (Atman).

commentary_faqs.question: Therapeutic & Somatic Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This practice is highly relevant to psychosomatic stability, stress management, building resilience against environmental stressors (thermal regulation/homeostasis), and treating anxiety by calming sensory overstimulation.

sanskrit_shloka:

तस्मात्प्रत्याहरेदेतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत् ॥
text:
मधुराम्लकतिक्तादिरसं गतं यदा मनः ।
तस्मात्प्रत्याहरेदेतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत् ॥

madhurāmlakatiktādirasaṃ gataṃ yadā manaḥ |
tasmātpratyāharedetadātmanyeva vaśaṃ nayet ||
translation: Whenever the mind wanders toward various tastes such as sweet, sour, or bitter, one should withdraw it from those objects and bring it under the direct control of the Self alone.

translations.author: English Translation

commentary_faqs.question: Practice: Pratyahara (specifically Rasana-indriya pratyahara or taste sensory withdrawal)
commentary_faqs.answer: Sensory withdrawal (Pratyahara) of the gustatory sense. The mind naturally runs toward tasty objects; practicing yoga involves consciously pulling the attention away from these external sensory inputs back to the internal Self (Atman).

commentary_faqs.question: Therapeutic & Somatic Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: Extremely relevant for treating modern lifestyle disorders like obesity, type 2 diabetes, eating disorders, and binge-eating habits. By cultivating sensory control over taste (rasendriya-jaya), patient awareness shifts from emotional eating to mindful nutrition.

sanskrit_shloka:
सुगन्धे वाऽपि दुर्गन्धे घ्राणेषु जायते मनः ।
तस्मात्प्रत्याहरेदेतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत् ॥
text:

तस्मात्प्रत्याहरेदेतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत् ॥
transliteration:
sugandhe vā'pi durgandhe ghrāṇeṣu jāyate manaḥ |
tasmātpratyāharedetadātmanyeva vaśaṁ nayet ||
translation: Whether in pleasant fragrance or in foul odor, the mind wanders through the sense of smell (olfactory organ). Therefore, one should withdraw the mind from those objects and bring it completely under control in the Self alone.

commentary_faqs.question: Practice: Ghrana Pratyahara (Olfactory sensory withdrawal)
commentary_faqs.answer: Pratyahara (sensory control and internalization of the mind from olfactory triggers into the internal Self).

commentary_faqs.question: Therapeutic & Somatic Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This practice acts as a highly effective therapy for sensory overstimulation, impulse control disorders, and addictive cravings (which are often triggered by olfactory cues). By strengthening conscious control over sensory inputs, it stabilizes the autonomic nervous system, decreases anxiety, and enhances mental focus.

translation: The knower of yoga, who is fully intent on the practice of sensory withdrawal (pratyāhāra), should restrain the senses which are naturally attached to sensory objects such as sound, and make them conform to the state of the mind.

commentary_faqs.question: Practice: Pratyahara
commentary_faqs.answer: Sensory restraint (Indriya Nigraha) and the redirection of the sensory energies to follow the path of the mind (Cittanucaritva), rather than external sensory objects.

commentary_faqs.question: Therapeutic & Somatic Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: Pratyahara practices (such as Shanmukhi Mudra, Yoga Nidra, and Antar Mouna) are highly effective in treating modern lifestyle diseases caused by chronic stress, sensory overload, anxiety disorders, attention deficits (ADHD), and mild hypertension, as they decouple the brain's stress response from constant external stimuli.

sanskrit_shloka:
वश्यता परमा तेन जायतेऽतिचलात्मनाम् ।
इन्द्रियाणामवश्यैस्तैर्न योगी योगसाधकः ॥
text:
वश्यता परमा तेन जायतेऽतिचलात्मनाम् ।
इन्द्रियाणामवश्यैस्तैर्न योगी योगसाधकः ॥
transliteration:
vaśyatā paramā tena jāyate'ticalātmanām |
indriyāṇāmavaśyaistairna yogī yogasādhakaḥ ||
translation: By that (practice of Pratyahara), supreme mastery is gained over the senses which are by nature extremely restless. Indeed, with those senses remaining uncontrolled, a yogi cannot become an achiever of Yoga.

commentary_faqs.question: Practice: Pratyahara
commentary_faqs.answer: Indriya-jaya (mastery over the senses) as an indispensable prerequisite for success in Yoga.

commentary_faqs.question: Therapeutic & Somatic Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: Pratyahara (sensory withdrawal and control) is crucial in modern yoga therapy for managing sensory overload, attention-deficit disorders (ADHD), anxiety, stress-induced disorders, and addictions. By pacifying the hyperactive senses, it downregulates the sympathetic nervous system and induces deep mental relaxation.

transliteration:
prāṇāyāmair dahed doṣān dhāraṇābhiś ca kilbiṣam |
pratyāhāreṇa viṣayān dhyānenānīśvarāṅ guṇān ||
translation: One should burn away physical and mental impurities through the practice of breath-control (pranayama), destroy sins and demerits through concentration (dharana), sever attachments to sensory objects through withdrawal of the senses (pratyahara), and dissolve non-divine or negative qualities through meditation (dhyana).

commentary_faqs.question: Practice: Pranayama, Dharana, Pratyahara, Dhyana
commentary_faqs.answer: The systematic purification of the body, mind, and spirit using the internal limbs of Yoga. Each limb targets a specific layer of impurity: Pranayama targets physiological and emotional blockages (Doshas), Dharana purifies the accumulation of past karmic demerits (Kilbisha), Pratyahara disconnects the consciousness from distracting sensory objects (Vishaya), and Dhyana dissolves non-divine, limiting egoic qualities (Anishvara Gunas).

commentary_faqs.question: Therapeutic & Somatic Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This sequential purification process holds immense therapeutic value in modern psychosomatic illness management. Pranayama helps regulate the autonomic nervous system, reducing chronic stress and system-wide inflammation (Doshas). Pratyahara acts as a sensory-detox mechanism crucial for treating modern addictions, anxiety, and attention deficit disorders by withdrawing the mind from overstimulation. Dhyana and Dharana restructure cognitive pathways, assisting in deep neurological rehabilitation and emotional regulation.

sanskrit_shloka: यथा पर्वतधातूनां दोषा दह्यन्ति धाम्यताम् । तथेन्द्रियकृता दोषा दह्यन्ते प्राणनिग्रहात् ॥
text: यथा पर्वतधातूनां दोषा दह्यन्ति धाम्यताम् । तथेन्द्रियकृता दोषा दह्यन्ते प्राणनिग्रहात् ॥
transliteration: yathā parvatadhātūnāṁ doṣā dahyanti dhāmyatām | tathendriyakṛtā doṣā dahyante prāṇanigrahāt ||
translation: Just as the impurities of metallic ores extracted from mountains are burnt away when they are smelted in a furnace, even so the impurities or defects caused by the senses are completely burnt away by the restraint of breath (Pranayama).

commentary_faqs.question: Practice: Pranayama (Prana-nigraha)
commentary_faqs.answer: Purification of sensory and mental impurities through breath regulation

commentary_faqs.question: Therapeutic & Somatic Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: Pranayama acts as a potent purifying mechanism, balancing the autonomic nervous system, reducing sympathetic dominance, and aiding in the therapy of lifestyle and psychosomatic disorders such as chronic stress, hypertension, anxiety, and metabolic syndromes by eliminating systemic 'toxins' (doshas).

sanskrit_shloka:
समः समासनो भूत्वा संहृत्य चरणावुभौ ।
संवृतास्यस्तथैवोरू सम्यग्विष्टभ्य चाग्रतः ॥

translation: Having assumed a balanced, steady seated posture (or Samasana) while keeping the torso erect, drawing both feet close together, keeping the mouth closed, and likewise firmly supporting both thighs in front.

commentary_faqs.question: Practice: Samasana / Meditative Seated Posture
commentary_faqs.answer: Physical alignment, spinal stability, and sensory containment (closing the mouth and positioning the limbs) as a foundation for Pratyahara (withdrawal of senses).

commentary_faqs.question: Therapeutic & Somatic Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This posture promotes optimal spinal alignment and pelvic stability, which relieves lower back pain, improves breathing efficiency, stabilizes the autonomic nervous system, and helps mitigate anxiety and stress-related conditions.

sanskrit_shloka:
पार्ष्णिभ्यां लिङ्गवृषणावस्पृशन्प्रयतः स्थितः ।
किञ्चिदुन्नामितशिरा दन्तैर्दन्तान्न संस्पृशेत् ।
संपश्यन्नासिकाग्रं स्वं दिशश्चानवलोकयन् ॥
text:
पार्ष्णिभ्यां लिङ्गवृषणावस्पृशन्प्रयतः स्थितः ।
किञ्चिदुन्नामितशिरा दन्तैर्दन्तान्न संस्पृशेत् ।
संपश्यन्नासिकाग्रं स्वं दिशश्चानवलोकयन् ॥
transliteration:
pārṣṇibhyāṃ liṅgavṛṣaṇāvaspṛśanprayataḥ sthitaḥ |
kiñcidunnāmitaśirā dantairdantānna saṃspṛśet |
sampaśyannāsikāgraṃ svaṃ diśaścānavalokayan ||
translation: Remaining self-controlled and steady, without touching the genitals (penis and scrotum) with both heels, holding the head slightly elevated, one should not let the upper and lower teeth touch each other. Gazing intently at the tip of one's own nose, and not looking around in any direction, [one should practice].

commentary_faqs.question: Practice: Pratyahara Sthiti (Preparatory Seated Posture & Nasikagra Drishti)
commentary_faqs.answer: Physical stabilization (Kaya Sthairyam), jaw relaxation, and sensory withdrawal (Pratyahara) through steady gaze and postural alignment.

commentary_faqs.question: Therapeutic & Somatic Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: Highly effective for relieving anxiety and stress. Keeping the teeth apart (not clenching) is a direct therapeutic application for relieving Temporomandibular Joint (TMJ) disorders and bruxism. Steady gazing (Nasikagra Drishti) trains neural pathways associated with sustained attention and parasympathetic dominance.

sanskrit_shloka:
रजसा तमसो वृत्तिं सत्त्वेन रजसस्तथा ।
सञ्चाद्य निर्मले सत्त्वे स्थितो युञ्जीत योगवित् ॥
text:

सञ्चाद्य निर्मले सत्त्वे स्थितो युञ्जीत योगवित् ॥

translation: Having subdued the active modifications of Tamas (inertia/darkness) by means of Rajas (dynamism/passion), and likewise subduing the modifications of Rajas by means of Sattva (purity/light), the knower of Yoga, established firmly in pure Sattva, should practice meditation.

commentary_faqs.question: Practice: Pratyahara
commentary_faqs.answer: Guna-Niyantrana (progressive sublimation of the three qualities of nature—Tamas to Rajas, Rajas to Sattva—to achieve mental clarity and stable meditation)

commentary_faqs.question: Therapeutic & Somatic Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This technique of progressive mental regulation serves as an effective psychotherapeutic tool for treating clinical depression and lethargy (by activating Rajasic energy) and subsequently managing anxiety, ADHD, and stress (by channeling Rajas into calm Sattvic mindfulness).

sanskrit_shloka:

निगृह्य समवायेन प्रत्याहारमुपक्रमेत् ॥

nigṛhya samavāyena pratyāhāramupakramet ||
translation: Having systematically restrained the senses from their respective sense objects, as well as the vital breaths (Prāṇa and others) and the mind, one should practice Pratyāhāra (sensory withdrawal).

commentary_faqs.question: Practice: Pratyahara
commentary_faqs.answer: Systematic withdrawal and internalization of the Indriyas (senses), Prana (vital energies), and Manas (mind) from external fields.

commentary_faqs.question: Therapeutic & Somatic Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This systematic internalization serves as an excellent therapy for modern stress, sensory overload, ADHD, and psychosomatic disorders by shifting the autonomic nervous system from sympathetic (fight-or-flight) to parasympathetic (rest-and-digest) dominance.

translation: He who indeed withdraws all desires, just as a tortoise retracts all its limbs, and who remains ever-delighted in the Self and established in the One, beholds the Self within the self.

commentary_faqs.question: Practice: Pratyahara
commentary_faqs.answer: Sensory withdrawal (Pratyahara) leading to Self-realization (Atmadarshana) using the classic metaphor of a tortoise

commentary_faqs.question: Therapeutic & Somatic Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: This practice helps in managing stress, anxiety, ADHD, and sensory overload by retraining the mind to withdraw from external sensory stimuli and quieten the sympathetic nervous system.

sanskrit_shloka: स बाह्याभ्यन्तरं शौचं निष्पाद्याकण्ठनाभितः । पूरयित्वा बुधो देहं प्रत्याहारमुपक्रमेत् ॥

commentary_faqs.question: Practice: Pratyahara with Kumbhaka (Breath Retention)
commentary_faqs.answer: Internal and external purification as a prerequisite for sensory withdrawal.

commentary_faqs.question: Therapeutic & Somatic Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: The practice of diaphragmatic breath control up to the throat facilitates autonomic nervous system regulation and parasympathetic activation, useful in managing anxiety and psychosomatic disorders.

sanskrit_shloka: तथा वै योगयुक्तस्य योगिनो नियतात्मनः । सर्वे दोषाः प्रणश्यन्ति स्वस्थश्चैवोपजायते ॥
text: तथा वै योगयुक्तस्य योगिनो नियतात्मनः । सर्वे दोषाः प्रणश्यन्ति स्वस्थश्चैवोपजायते ॥
transliteration: tathā vai yogayuktasya yogino niyatātmanaḥ | sarve doṣāḥ praṇaśyanti svasthaścaivopajāyate ||
translation: Thus, indeed, for the yogi who is united in yoga and whose self is controlled, all defects vanish, and he becomes established in his own self (health/equilibrium).

translations.author: Hindi Translation (भावार्थ)
translations.description: इस प्रकार, वास्तव में जो योगी योग से युक्त है और जिसका मन अपने वश में है, उसके सभी दोष नष्ट हो जाते हैं और वह अपनी वास्तविक स्वस्थ स्थिति को प्राप्त कर लेता है।

commentary_faqs.question: Practice: Pratyahara and Dhyana
commentary_faqs.answer: Svasthya (True Health) as the state of equilibrium achieved through Yoga

commentary_faqs.question: Therapeutic & Somatic Significance
commentary_faqs.answer: The verse indicates that yoga practice acts as a remedial measure to eliminate metabolic, psychological, and physiological defects (Doshas), promoting homeostasis.
